nameStory: Rathkea octopunctata gets its species name 'octopunctata' from Latin, meaning 'eight-spotted,' referring to the eight distinctive spots often visible on its bell-shaped body. The genus name Rathkea honors Heinrich Rathke, a 19th-century German biologist who made important contributions to understanding marine invertebrates. This tiny hydrozoan carries the legacy of early marine researchers in its scientific name.
description: Rathkea octopunctata is a small hydrozoan, a type of marine animal related to jellyfish and sea anemones. It has a translucent, bell-shaped body called a medusa that pulses gently through the water. The creature is quite tiny, typically measuring less than half an inch across its bell. Like other hydrozoans, it has tentacles hanging from its bell margin and feeds on tiny plankton and small marine organisms.

idTips.label: Eight spots pattern
idTips.description: Look for eight dark spots arranged around the bell margin - these may appear as brownish or reddish marks that stand out against the translucent body

idTips.label: Bell shape
idTips.description: The body forms a small, dome-like bell that's nearly transparent and feels gelatinous if gently touched

idTips.label: Tentacle arrangement
idTips.description: Multiple thin tentacles trail from the bell's edge, often appearing to flow gracefully as the animal moves

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small - the entire bell typically measures less than 12mm (about half an inch) across

idTips.label: Swimming motion
idTips.description: Moves with gentle, rhythmic pulsing contractions of the bell, creating a graceful bobbing motion through the water

habitat: Found in coastal New England waters, particularly in shallow marine environments like tide pools, harbors, and protected bays. This species prefers areas with moderate water movement where it can drift and hunt for small plankton. It's most commonly encountered in the warmer months when plankton populations are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Begin appearing in warmer coastal waters as temperatures rise and plankton blooms start to develop.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during summer months when water temperatures are warmest and food sources are most plentiful.
seasonality.fall: May still be present in early fall but become less common as water temperatures begin to drop.
seasonality.winter: Generally absent from New England waters during the coldest months, likely retreating to deeper or warmer waters.

funFact: Despite being an extremely rare find in New England waters with only one recorded observation, Rathkea octopunctata can reproduce both sexually and asexually - it can clone itself when conditions are favorable, potentially creating identical copies without needing a mate!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small jellyfish or hydrozoans, but the distinctive pattern of eight spots around the bell margin is unique. Most other small jellyfish in New England waters lack this specific spotted pattern - count the spots carefully to confirm identification.
contextualKnowledge: This species is extremely rare in New England waters, with scientific records showing only a single documented observation in the region. Finding one would be considered a significant discovery and should be reported to local marine biologists or naturalist organizations.
compareHints: Since Rathkea octopunctata appears to be the only species of its genus documented in New England, compare it with other small hydrozoans in the region. Unlike most other small jellyfish, Rathkea has the distinctive eight-spot pattern that gives it its name. Other small hydrozoans typically lack this organized spotting pattern and may have different tentacle arrangements or bell proportions.
